Trask Performance’s 180-HP Nickel-Plated M8 FXR Is a Street Eater

HOTBIKESTAFF

Photos: Alex Chapman

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 3:36
Instaread

Some custom motorcycles are built to sit under show lights. Charlie Brown’s nickel-plated Trask Performance FXR was built to do much more than that. With a 143ci Ward Performance Milwaukee-Eight engine making nearly 180 horsepower at the rear wheel, this 1987 FXR blends show-bike detail with real street-bike aggression.

The first thing that grabs your eye is the finish. Instead of following the chrome-heavy FXR crowd, Brown wanted something different. Every visible metal component was polished and nickel plated, giving the bike a warmer, slightly yellow tint that contrasts perfectly against the satin-black bodywork, exposed carbon fiber, and blacked-out performance parts.

“I wanted that yellow tint,” Brown said. “There are plenty of chrome FXRs out there. I wanted something different.”

Brown’s relationship with Trask Performance goes back nearly 20 years. He first met Nick Trask in 2006 after buying a new Harley-Davidson Fat Boy and needing a dyno tune. What started as a customer relationship grew into a long-running friendship, with Trask helping Brown build several bikes over the years, including an award-winning 1988 FXR.

Inside Trask Performance, Brown even earned the nickname “80 Percent.”

“He’ll put together the bike a lot of the way,” Trask Service Manager Moots McDonagh said. “Then when it comes to wiring, machining, fabrication, and the details that make everything work, he brings it to us to finish.”

That nickname fit this FXR perfectly. Brown started with little more than a title and a plan. Working with Chris and Justin at FXR Division, he sourced a titled FXR frame that could accept a Milwaukee-Eight engine. Since almost everything would be replaced, there was no need to begin with a complete donor bike.

Brown collected parts for months, then delivered a rolling chassis, boxes of components, and an early Ward Performance 143ci engine package to Trask Performance in Phoenix. From there, Moots transformed the pile of parts into one brutally refined performance FXR.

The engine combination includes Ward Performance cylinders and heads, S&S cases, a Darkhorse Man-O-War crankshaft, Carrillo rods, a 64mm Screamin’ Eagle throttle body, ThunderMax ECM, Ward 143S cam, Trask Big Papi air cleaner, and a one-off Trask Performance exhaust.

Getting it all to work took serious effort.

“We totally redid the wiring,” Moots said. “We got it working, fired it up, did heat cycles, put it on the dyno, and made it run.”

The result is a claimed 180-horsepower rear-wheel monster riding on a relatively narrow 150-series rear tire. Brown admits the bike can get wild when pushed.

“It’s fun and a little erratic sometimes,” he joked.

But this FXR isn’t just about horsepower. The chassis package includes Rebuffini/Öhlins front suspension, Öhlins Blackline rear shocks with FXR Division extensions, Rebuffini radial calipers, Lyndall B-52 Crown Cut rotors, Jade Affiliated x San Diego Customs wheels, Alloy Art swingarm, and a long list of FXR Division, TPJ, OG Moto, Saddlemen, and Trask components.

From the carbon-fiber bodywork and Saddlemen mini fairing to the OG Moto risers, Trask LED headlight, Bullitworx tank, and custom Rolling Art paint, every detail works together. Nothing feels random. Nothing feels overdone.

For Brown, the real value is in the people behind the build. This FXR represents nearly two decades of friendship, trust, and shared performance obsession between one dedicated owner and one of the most respected Harley performance shops in the country.

The finished bike is more than a nickel-plated showpiece. It’s one of the most striking modern FXRs to roll out of Trask Performance—and with 180 horsepower on tap, it has the bite to back up every bit of its shine.
